cues.text: Section six is the practical lab.
This is where the software-defined networking ideas become something you can try yourself, in a controlled environment.
The tools are Mininet and Open vSwitch, running inside an isolated Ubuntu machine, together with a compatible Ryu controller.
Mininet emulates hosts and switches on a single machine.
Open vSwitch is the software switch that speaks OpenFlow.
Ryu is the controller, the program that decides how the switch should handle traffic.
The word isolated matters.
Run this in a dedicated teaching virtual machine, not on a network you depend on.
The example topology is deliberately small: two hosts and one switch.
Both hosts attach to the switch, and the switch connects to the controller.
Here is the command sequence.
The first line is a comment: in an isolated teaching VM, the controller process is separately running.
So start your Ryu controller first, in its own process, before launching Mininet.
Then the command is: sudo mn, space, dash dash topo, single comma 2, space, dash dash switch, ovsk comma protocols equals OpenFlow13, then a backslash to continue on the next line.
The continuation reads: dash dash controller, remote comma ip equals 127.0.0.1 comma port equals 6653.
Taking those parts in turn.
The sudo mn part launches Mininet with administrator rights, which it needs to create virtual network devices.
The dash dash topo single comma 2 option selects the single-switch topology with two hosts attached.
The dash dash switch ovsk option selects the Open vSwitch kernel-mode switch, and protocols equals OpenFlow13 restricts it to OpenFlow version 1.3.
The dash dash controller remote option tells Mininet not to start its own controller.
It connects to an external one instead, at IP address 127.0.0.1, which is the local loopback address, on port 6653.
Port 6653 is the OpenFlow controller port.
Next comes the comment: Mininet CLI.
Inside the Mininet command line, you type pingall.
This makes every host try to ping every other host, so it tests connectivity between your two hosts.
It also drives the learning behaviour in the controller, because the first packets are what the switch has to ask about.
Then the comment: separate terminal.
In another terminal, run: sudo ovs-ofctl, space, dash O, space, OpenFlow13, space, dump-flows, space, s1.
This asks Open vSwitch to print the flow table of the switch named s1, using OpenFlow 1.3.
That is how you see which rules are installed on the switch.
Now the conditions and the exercises.
A suitable learning-switch or controller application must be configured.
A learning switch is a controller app that learns which MAC address sits behind which port.
Versions and dependencies may vary, so expect to adjust things to match your own installation of Ryu, Open vSwitch and Mininet.
Then there is a sequence of tasks.
First, inspect packet-in and flow installation.
A packet-in is the message the switch sends to the controller when a packet matches no existing flow rule.
Look at how the controller reacts and what flow entries it installs afterwards.
Second, implement and test guest isolation and a permitted flow.
Guest isolation means blocking a guest host from reaching protected resources.
The permitted flow is the specific traffic you deliberately allow.
Test both, so you confirm that the blocked traffic is blocked and the allowed traffic works.
Third, disconnect the controller in the lab and observe the actual fail-mode.
Fail-mode is how the switch behaves when it loses contact with its controller.
Observe what really happens in your setup rather than assuming.
Fourth, restore the controller connection and verify that normal behaviour returns.
Finally, integrate an IoT edge segment, with specific service access and local processing.
That means a group of IoT devices that can reach only the services they actually need, with processing kept local at the edge.
And avoid treating controller reachability as a requirement for every local packet if the flows are already installed.
Once the rules are in the switch, packets that match them are forwarded by the switch itself, without asking the controller each time.
Local traffic need not stop merely because the controller is briefly unreachable.
One last point.
The source makes no execution claim.
These commands are presented as a lab to run and observe, not as results that have already been obtained.
